To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
vitamin A kinetics in healthy young adults were best modeled using the same model that was previously developed using data from older adults with higher stores of vitamin A.

the vitamin A kinetics in young adults with low vitamin A stores were best described by the same model that we previously developed by using kinetic data for older adults, with differences in parameter values reflecting differences in vitamin A stores; and that the relative β-carotence bioefficacy estimated by using the WinSAAM model was similar to previously reported values but with high interindividual variation.

the kinetics of vitamin A are best described by a 6-compartment model in healthy young adults of moderate vitamin A status and that the relative bioefficacy of β-carotene in this group of individuals is 13.5%, with high interindividual variation.

the results of this study provide evidence that the relative bioefficacy of β-carotene as a source of vitamin A is lower than that of retinol, but is not as low as previously thought, and that the bioefficacy varies considerably between individuals.

the results of the current study provide further evidence that β-carotene does not have a major role in the maintenance of vitamin A status in humans, and the results of the present study support this conclusion.

the model-based approach to the analysis of plasma retinol and β-carotene kinetics is a powerful and flexible method for estimating the parameters of vitamin A metabolism and for quantifying β-carotene efficacy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the WinSAAM software can be used to analyze kinetic data on plasma vitamin A kinetics in young adults and to estimate relative β-carotence bioefficacy.
model-based compartmental analysis provides a unique opportunity to estimate vitamin A kinetics in healthy adults and to determine relative provitamin A carotenoid bioefficacy in a single study.
the WinSAAM software can be used for compartmental analysis of plasma retinol data to quantify whole-body vitamin A kinetics and to estimate β-carotene relative bioefficacy.
